# Introduction

RhyME is an R package for detecting circadian rhythms in DNA methylation
data. It fits beta-regression cosinor models to methylation beta values. The package supports independent samples and
repeated measurements from the same subjects, with optional covariates
such as age and sex. An empirical Bayes (EB) prior can improve the
stability of precision estimates across CpGs.

RhyME identifies rhythmic CpG sites and estimates their amplitude, peak
time, and mean methylation level. This vignette walks through installation,
data preparation, model fitting, viewing results, and plotting fitted curves.

# Installation

Install the package:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("RhyME")
```


# Simulation example

## Simulation settings

This example uses simulated data with 15 subjects,
112 observed sampling records across nine planned time points,
and 2,000 CpGs comprising 200 rhythmic and 1,800 non-rhythmic sites.
Baseline methylation, precision, subject-level random-intercept variability,
and phase were jointly sampled from rows of CpG-specific parameter
estimates obtained from the real dataset. The logit-scale amplitude was
fixed at 0.09 for rhythmic sites and zero for non-rhythmic sites.
The parameter subset and sampling design are bundled in
`inst/extdata/example_parameters.rds`. Run `inst/scripts/make_example_data.R`
to regenerate the example; `inst/scripts/README` describes the inputs and usage.

```{r data}
library(RhyME)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(BiocParallel)

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "example_data.rds",
    package = "RhyME"))
se <- example$se
dim(se)
head(colData(se))
```



## Fit the model

For these repeated measurements, specify `subject_col` to include a random
intercept per subject. The default `prior = "auto"` estimates an empirical Bayes
prior from the data. Set `period` to the rhythm length in hours and the default is 24.
Sampling times can be irregular or span several days.

```{r fit}
fit <- fitCosinor(se, subject_col = "subject", prior = "auto", BPPARAM = SerialParam())
```


## View results

Results are stored in `rowData(fit)` with the `RhyME_` prefix.
Here we view the first two rhythmic and first two non-rhythmic CpGs,
including their detection results and estimated rhythm parameters.

```{r results}
result <- rowData(fit)
truth <- result$true_status == "Rhythmic"
selected_cpgs <- rownames(fit)[c(head(which(truth), 2),
    head(which(!truth), 2))]

columns <- c("true_status", "RhyME_pvalue", "RhyME_padj",
    "RhyME_amplitude", "RhyME_phase", "RhyME_mesor",
    "RhyME_converged")
result[selected_cpgs, columns]
```

The rhythm summaries describe the fitted mean curve on the beta-value scale.
For models with a subject random intercept, they are population-averaged
quantities obtained by marginalizing over the fitted random-intercept distribution.

- `RhyME_amplitude`: half the fitted peak-to-trough difference on the beta-value scale.
- `RhyME_phase`: peak time in hours, between 0 and `period`, relative to the input time origin.
- `RhyME_mesor`: fitted mean methylation level averaged over one period.



Select CpGs with BH-adjusted p-values below 0.05:

```{r significant}
detected <- result$RhyME_padj < 0.05
significant <- result[detected, , drop = FALSE]
nrow(significant)
```

The simulation labels in `rowData()` are annotations and are not used to fit
the model. Below, we compare the calls from each method with these labels.

View the fitting summary and estimated EB prior:

```{r summary}
metadata(fit)$RhyME$fitSummary
metadata(fit)$RhyME$ebPrior
```

## Run MetaCycle and compare calls with simulation truth

MetaCycle is an R package for detecting rhythmic signals in time-series data using ARSER, JTK_CYCLE,
and Lomb–Scargle (LS). For the replicated observations at regularly spaced time points in this example,
its default meta2d() strategy selects JTK_CYCLE and LS and combines their p-values using Fisher’s method.
We specify a 24-hour period to match RhyME. Here, meta2d() uses the sampling times without modeling
within-subject correlation, whereas RhyME includes a subject-specific random intercept.
We compare the resulting rhythmicity calls with the known simulation truth.

RhyME also uses beta regression to model the dependence of conditional variance
on mean methylation. Its empirical Bayes prior shares information across CpGs
to stabilize precision estimates.

```{r metacycle, results='hide'}
Y <- data.frame(CycID = rownames(se), assay(se))
meta_fit <- MetaCycle::meta2d(
    infile = "simulated_beta", inDF = Y, filestyle = "csv",
    timepoints = se$time, minper = 24, maxper = 24,
    outputFile = FALSE)
meta_result <- meta_fit$meta
```

```{r align-metacycle, include=FALSE}
meta_result <- meta_result[match(rownames(se), meta_result$CycID), ]
```

Apply BH adjustment separately for each method across all
2,000 CpGs and use the same threshold of 0.05. The table compares known
truth with detection: TP and FN are the detected and missed rhythmic CpGs;
FP and TN are the non-rhythmic CpGs called rhythmic and not called rhythmic.
Power is TP / 200, and the observed FDP is FP / (TP + FP).

```{r method-comparison, echo=FALSE}
pvalues <- data.frame(
    RhyME = result$RhyME_pvalue,
    JTK = meta_result$JTK_pvalue,
    LS = meta_result$LS_pvalue,
    MetaCycle = meta_result$meta2d_pvalue)
padj <- sapply(pvalues, p.adjust, method = "BH")
rownames(padj) <- rownames(se)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(padj), function(method) {
    called <- !is.na(padj[, method]) & padj[, method] < 0.05
    tp <- sum(called & truth)
    fp <- sum(called & !truth)
    data.frame(Method = method, TP = tp, FN = sum(truth) - tp,
        FP = fp, TN = sum(!truth) - fp,
        `Power (%)` = 100 * tp / sum(truth),
        `Observed FDP (%)` = if (sum(called)) 100 * fp / sum(called) else NA_real_,
        check.names = FALSE)
}))
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2),
    row.names = FALSE, caption = "Known simulation truth versus calls at BH < 0.05.")
```


## Plot fitted curves

Plot the same four loci shown in the result table. Points are observed beta
values, including between-subject variation, and red lines are fitted
population-averaged mean curves. The first two panels are rhythmic loci;
the last two are non-rhythmic. Each panel shows the locus ID from the table
and uses its own beta-value range to show small changes.

```{r plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
plotCosinorFit(fit, cpgs = selected_cpgs, ncol = 2) +
    ggplot2::theme_gray()
```


# Prepare your own data

Use a numeric matrix of beta values after quality control and normalization,
with CpGs in rows and samples in columns. Sample metadata should contain
collection time in hours and, for repeated measurements, a subject identifier.
CpG and sample names should be unique, and sample names must match between
the matrix and metadata.

For example, read two CSV files whose first columns contain row names:

```{r own-data, eval=FALSE}
beta <- as.matrix(read.csv("beta_values.csv", row.names = 1,
    check.names = FALSE))
sample_info <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv", row.names = 1)
sample_info <- sample_info[colnames(beta), , drop = FALSE]

se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(beta = beta),
    colData = DataFrame(sample_info))
```

Alternatively, extract beta values from a preprocessed `minfi`
`GenomicRatioSet`, retaining genomic coordinates and sample metadata:

```{r minfi-input, eval=FALSE}
se <- SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(beta = minfi::getBeta(grSet)),
    rowRanges = rowRanges(grSet),
    colData = colData(grSet))
```

For either input, use `assay_name = "beta"` in `fitCosinor()`.
Missing beta values are allowed, but collection time, subject identifiers
when required, and any adjustment covariates must be present and complete
in `colData(se)`.

# Other options
## Independent samples and the default fit

For independent samples, omit `subject_col`. The bundled example also contains
independent observations for 1,200 of the same CpGs, with 48 samples at six
collection times and no subject effects.

```{r fixed-default}
se_independent <- example$se_independent
fit_fixed <- fitCosinor(se_independent, BPPARAM = SerialParam())
metadata(fit_fixed)$RhyME$ebPrior
```

## Adjust for covariates

Add covariates to colData() and pass their column names. Numeric and
categorical variables are supported. Here we assign illustrative ages to
subjects and analyze 25 rhythmic and 25 non-rhythmic CpGs. We use prior = "none"
because this small subset provides limited information for estimating the empirical Bayes prior.

```{r covariates}
subject_age <- setNames(seq(28, 56, by = 2), levels(se$subject))
se$age <- unname(subject_age[as.character(se$subject)])
i <- c(head(which(truth), 25), head(which(!truth), 25))
adjusted <- fitCosinor(se[i, ],
    time_col = "time", subject_col = "subject", covariates = "age",
    prior = "none", BPPARAM = SerialParam(), verbose = FALSE)
```

For multiple covariates, use `covariates = c("age", "sex")` when both
columns are present. Do not include the subject identifier as a covariate.
